verdict: Avoid new pharma/API exposure in Visakhapatnam for now; lend only to the strongest formulation-linked units with tight structure, and decline small single-customer API and CRO borrowers.
title: Visakhapatnam Pharmaceuticals & APIs: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**An API or formulation unit here is a chemistry plant that converts solvents, intermediates and power into batches of regulated product, and gets paid only after the batch clears the buyer's quality gate.** Cash sits in inventory (raw material, in-process, finished awaiting release) and in receivables from a handful of large buyers; the plant itself is heavy capex with effluent treatment and power as fixed costs. Rating reports on peers show exactly this: working capital intensity of 52% in FY2019, 47% in FY2020 and 48% in 7MFY2021, down from 77% in FY2018, and still described as high [10]. So when a proposal lands, check the receivables-and-inventory days against these peer levels; if the borrower's working capital intensity is above the peer range, ask for the buyer-wise ageing and the batch-release calendar before sizing the limit.

## What has changed now
**The local demand signal is weak even as the national pharma peer set is printing record numbers.** Andhra Pradesh GST collections are -0.2% Apr-to-date against India +6.1%, 6.3 pp slower [D], and India-wide output is -2.1% Apr-to-date [D] while bank credit runs +21.6% YoY [D] — credit is outrunning real output. Against that, peers are strong: Aarti Pharmalabs reported record quarterly revenue of Rs. 613 crore, up 47% YoY, with EBITDA margin at 22.2% from 17.7% [4][6], and RPG Life Sciences targets 25% API growth [5]. Read this as a split market: large, diversified, export-linked players are doing well; the local small unit is not automatically carried by that.

## Where the growth is
**Pursue formulation-linked and CDMO/contract-manufacturing borrowers with more than one qualified buyer, not single-customer API shops.** The API industry grew at 8.4% CAGR between CY2017 and CY2022E and is expected at ~7% ahead, with China at 65-70% of India's API imports and global buyers diversifying supply chains [11] — that diversification is the real opportunity, and it lands with units that already hold approvals. Note the local source is thin: a directory lists 11 pharma companies in the city including Divi's, Laurus, Lupin, Gland and Hetero [1], but it gives no financials, so lean on first principles and the peer and rating evidence. Avoid small CRO-dependent units: one rated peer at Rs. 61.0 crore FY2024 revenue saw demand from US clients weaken, with high customer concentration [8].

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the working-capital cycle, not the plant.** Take monthly stock-and-receivable statements, buyer-wise sales, and power consumption; the state's electricity demand is +18.1% Apr-to-date versus India +9.5% [D], so a unit running below that trend is suspect. Covenant on working capital intensity and on customer concentration; for capex, tie drawdown to commissioning. Collect from customer the actual receivable days, inventory days and buyer concentration before any sanction.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch receivable stretch and buyer loss first.** A single large buyer delaying release, inventory days climbing past the peer 48% intensity [10], or power consumption falling while sales are reported up are all exit signals. Rating evidence is old — the ICRA and CARE reports carry no clear date and reference FY2024 and earlier [8][9][10] — so treat them as structure guides, not current numbers.
watch: Monthly buyer-wise sales and receivable ageing (monthly)
Top buyer share rises or ageing crosses peer intensity -> freeze enhancement, seek collateral
Consumption falls while sales rise -> ask for batch records, reduce limit
Filing gap or falling GST vs AP -0.2% trend [D] -> escalate, review account
Inventory days climb above peer 48% [10] -> reprice or trim drawing power
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
